_note: SAMPLE recap content, generated from the hypothesised draft.

feature.headline: Twelve Men Enter, Nobody Improves
feature.standfirst: Fifteen rounds in The Lab Rats produced one quarterback hoarder, one tight end cult, and a kicker taken with an entire NFL roster still breathing on the board.

sections.heading: Mike Built A Quarterback Room
body: Jalen Hurts, Drake Maye, Dak Prescott, Jaxson Dart, Daniel Jones. Five quarterbacks in six rounds in a league that starts two. Mike isn't drafting a fantasy team, he's running a training camp, and by round six he was taking Daniel Jones like a man who'd already checked the other four for a limp.

Keshia looked at that and decided it wasn't enough. Josh Allen, Stafford, Caleb Williams, Goff, and Tyler Shough — a rookie's rookie — off the board before round seven. Between the two of them they took ten quarterbacks and can start four. Somewhere out there a manager who needs a second starter is refreshing waivers and finding Jarrett Stidham.

sections.heading: Bree's Bad Boys Play Tight End
body: Tyler Warren, Colston Loveland, Sam LaPorta, and Greg Dulcich. Four tight ends for one tight end slot, and three of them are guys you draft because somebody told you the arrow's pointing up. Bree started with three receivers, then apparently decided the fastest way to win a superflex league was a formation with no quarterbacks in it.

Because there's one. Sam Darnold, round six, and that's the whole plan. Every Sunday Bree gets to watch Darnold do whatever Darnold does that week, and then look down her bench at four tight ends who can't legally throw it.

sections.heading: Colin Went Shopping For Tight Ends Too
body: Travis Kelce, Mark Andrews, Isaiah Likely, AJ Barner. Colin took Kelce, then took the guy who'd back up Kelce, then took the guy who backs up the guy he already had in Andrews. He's not building a lineup, he's collecting the entire position like a man completing a set.

And the quarterbacks? Jordan Love and Malik Willis. In a format that starts two, Colin's second starter is a career backup, which he handled by drafting three more tight ends afterward. The plan is to out-block everyone.

sections.heading: Jesse Stopped At The Pharmacy
body: Jesse took three quarterbacks in three straight rounds — Purdy, Kyler, Baker — like a man who'd been burned before and wasn't going to let it happen twice. Fine. Then the running backs started arriving and they all had paperwork.

Jonathon Brooks, coming off knees that have been rebuilt more than once. Tyjae Spears. Jadarian Price. Josh Jacobs in the tenth as the healthy one, which tells you everything about the rest of the room. Jesse spent the back half of his draft assembling a depth chart you could stand up in a waiting room.

sections.heading: Doug Cornered The Running Back Market
body: Bijan Robinson, Jeremiyah Love, Kyren Williams, Bucky Irving, Bhayshul Tuten, J.K. Dobbins, Rachaad White. Seven running backs. Doug looked at a five-man bench and thought: what if all of them were the same guy. Every Sunday he picks four to start and tells the other three it's a numbers thing.

The quarterbacks are Jayden Daniels and Bryce Young, which in a superflex league is one answer and one question. And then in round twelve, with the roster already stacked eight deep at one position, he took Jalen Nailor. Twenty-nine better guys still there. He wasn't drafting a receiver, he was drafting a name he half-remembered from a Thursday night.

sections.heading: Evan And Chenell Just Drafted Well
body: Evan took James Cook and De'Von Achane back-to-back at the turn, then Mahomes, then Brock Bowers, and never once reached for anybody. Fifteen picks, almost all of them the best player sitting there. Aaron Rodgers in the eleventh as a QB2 is the only whiff of chaos in the whole thing, and even that's just a guy hedging his bets with a Hall of Famer.

Chenell won it last year and drafted like somebody who'd read the receipt. McCaffrey, Breece Hall, Nico Collins, A.J. Brown, Kittle. Solid, boring, and lethal. Both of them will spend September pretending this is hard.

sections.heading: The Kicker Round Was A Bloodbath
body: Six managers took a kicker. Every single one of them did it with about seven hundred and ninety better players still on the board. Jesse got Brandon Aubrey, Doug got Cameron Dicker, Keshia got Harrison Mevis. Nobody kicked the tires. They just needed the slot filled and the draft to end.

Same story with defenses. Chargers, Chiefs, Patriots, Browns, Eagles, Lions, Ravens, Rams, Seahawks, Steelers, Texans, Broncos — twelve managers, twelve units, all taken in the same round with hundreds of real football players still sitting there. It's the one moment in the draft where everybody's strategy aligns perfectly, and the strategy is exhaustion.

teams.verdict: Three quarterbacks, none of them good
teams.teaser: Jesse collected quarterbacks like a man who'd heard the word once and liked the sound of it.
body: Gibbs at 1.01 is the last clean thing on this roster. After that Jesse went out and got Brock Purdy, Kyler Murray and Baker Mayfield in three straight swings, which isn't a quarterback room so much as a support group. Superflex starts two. He's got three, and every Sunday one of them sits on the bench being told he's still part of the plan.

Then the running backs. Etienne, Jadarian Price, Jonathon Brooks, Josh Jacobs, Tyjae Spears. Brooks is coming off two torn ACLs and Jesse wanted him badly enough to walk past five healthier guys to get there. He's not building depth, he's building a waiting room, and Spears in the thirteenth is the last chair in it. Mike Evans and Ladd McConkey are the only receivers here worth starting, which in a league that starts three is a problem he plans to solve by not thinking about it.

And then the kicker. Brandon Aubrey, taken 790 places ahead of where the board said, with a Chargers defense right before him for company. Two picks, both of which could've been made in your sleep on Saturday morning, both of which Jesse spent real capital on. Somewhere a startable receiver is still sitting there wondering what he did.

teams.teaser: Doug drafted eight running backs and two receivers who matter, then bought a kicker to celebrate.
body: Bijan first, fine. Jeremiyah Love, Kyren Williams, Bucky Irving, Bhayshul Tuten, J.K. Dobbins, Rachaad White. That's seven running backs before the twelfth round in a format with two RB slots and five bench spots. Doug didn't draft a roster, he cornered a position, and the position doesn't know he did it. Dobbins in the ninth is the tell — a guy whose entire career has been an injury report with a highlight attached, and Doug looked at that and thought: depth chart.

The receivers are the horror. Rashee Rice, then a long quiet nothing until Stefon Diggs in the tenth, Jalen Nailor in the twelfth, De'Zhaun Stribling in the thirteenth. He starts three receivers a week. He owns roughly three receivers. The margin for a hamstring is zero, and Doug has spent the whole draft acting like hamstrings are somebody else's problem.

Quarterback: Jayden Daniels and Bryce Young. Superflex demands two starters and Doug found the one pairing where the second slot is a dare. Every Sunday he gets to choose which four running backs don't play, and he'll enjoy it, because choosing is the only part of this he's good at.

teams.verdict: Cornering a market that doesn't exist
teams.teaser: Five quarterbacks, three tight ends, and one lonely running back trying to hold the whole thing up.
body: Josh Allen, Stafford, Caleb Williams, Goff, Tyler Shough. Five quarterbacks in a format that starts two. Keshia isn't drafting, she's hoarding, and the last one is a rookie who has to beat out a guy on his own roster before he beats out anybody else's. Shough in the sixth is the pick where a hobby becomes a condition.

Then she did it again at tight end. Kyle Pitts, Dalton Kincaid, Brenton Strange. Pitts has been the next big thing for four seasons and produced in none of them, Kincaid catches a pass and then a trainer, and Strange is there because the shelf still had room. One tight end slot. Three tight ends. The second warehouse opens in the eleventh.

Ashton Jeanty and Jordan Mason are the running backs. That's it. That's the entire ground game for sixteen weeks, and Mason arrived in the tenth round as an afterthought. Courtland Sutton and Khalil Shakir hold up the receiver room by themselves. Somewhere in this roster there's a very good football team, and it's buried under four backup quarterbacks nobody will ever start.

teams.verdict: The champ drafted like a champ, sadly
teams.teaser: Chenell built the most sensible roster here, which on this page is its own kind of failure.
body: McCaffrey and Breece Hall, then Nico Collins, A.J. Brown, DK Metcalf and George Kittle. It's balanced. It's mean. The receiver room could start for anyone and the tight end is the guy other tight ends watch film of. Nothing about this is funny, which is the most annoying thing a defending champion can do.

The one soft spot is under center. Geno Smith in the ninth and Cam Ward in the twelfth is a superflex quarterback plan built entirely on hope and a rookie. Ward has thrown professional passes for one season, and Chenell is asking him to start half the time. Every other week the roster is a title contender and a guy who might get benched by Thanksgiving.

Cam Skattebo, Jaylen Warren and Kenny Gainwell round out the backfield behind McCaffrey, which is fine, and Chig Okonkwo is a perfectly reasonable thirteenth-rounder, which is worse than fine, it's tidy. Chenell walked in, took good players at the right times, and left. No hoarding, no rehab wing, no kicker crimes beyond the mandatory ones. Whoever she is on draft night, she isn't giving anyone anything to work with.

teams.verdict: Four tight ends and one quarterback
teams.teaser: Bree assembled the finest collection of tight ends in the league, which is like winning a hot dog eating contest.
body: Puka Nacua, CeeDee Lamb, Chris Olave. Great start. Then Tyler Warren in the fourth, Colston Loveland in the fifth, Sam LaPorta in the seventh, and Greg Dulcich in the thirteenth for reasons only Bree can explain. One tight end starts. Four are rostered. She's not building a lineup, she's stocking a position group for a team that plays two-tight-end sets in her imagination.

Quarterback: Sam Darnold. That's the list. In superflex. In a format where two of them play every week, Bree has one guy, and it's the one who spent most of his career being handed a clipboard. The second quarterback slot is going to sit there empty every Sunday like a chair nobody claimed at dinner.

The backfield is Rico Dowdle, Kyle Monangai, Aaron Jones and Jacory Croskey-Merritt, which is four names and no answer. Meanwhile the tight end wing keeps expanding. By the thirteenth round Dulcich walks in and there's genuinely nowhere to put him. Somewhere on Bree's roster page is a slot marked QB2 that has never known love.

teams.verdict: One quarterback, four tight ends, zero sense
teams.teaser: Jay took C.J. Stroud and then acted like the quarterback problem in a superflex league had been fully addressed.
body: The first six picks are gorgeous. Jonathan Taylor, Kenneth Walker, Chase Brown, Drake London, Malik Nabers, DeVonta Smith. Real players, real production, nothing to say. Then Jay looked at his roster, saw two empty quarterback slots, and drafted a tight end.

C.J. Stroud eventually shows up in the eighth and is the only quarterback on the roster. In superflex. Jay is going to start Stroud and then a running back in the flex every single week while eleven other guys start two passers, and he'll do it with the calm of a man who's certain the rules changed and nobody told the league.

And then the tight ends arrive like a family reunion. Tucker Kraft in the seventh, Evan Engram in the eleventh, Darren Waller in the thirteenth — Waller, who's spent recent years mostly deciding whether to keep playing at all. Three tight ends, one slot, and Jay burned an eleventh-round pick to make sure the bench was covered at a position he can only use once. Xavier Worthy and Calvin Ridley are stacked on top of six other receivers he already owns. He'll spend September moving guys around a lineup that has one hole and no one to put in it.

teams.teaser: Tyler drafted a wide receiver corps so deep that eight of them will never play a snap for him.
body: Ja'Marr Chase and Justin Jefferson is the best start on the board. Then DJ Moore, Zay Flowers, Jameson Williams, Wan'Dale Robinson, Rashid Shaheed. Seven receivers. Three slots. Tyler kept going back to the same aisle in the same store expecting the shelves to change, and every time he came out with another slot receiver.

The running back situation is Chuba Hubbard. That's not the top of the depth chart, that's the whole chart, taken in the ninth round like a chore he'd been putting off. Two RB slots and one guy to fill them means Tyler will spend Sunday mornings staring at a lineup card, then plugging in a fourth receiver and calling it strategy.

Then, having ignored the backfield entirely, he bought three tight ends — Jake Ferguson, Juwan Johnson, and Terrance Ferguson, a rookie, in the eleventh. There's one tight end slot. There are two Fergusons. Trevor Lawrence and Justin Herbert at least cover superflex, which makes this the rare roster where the quarterbacks are the least confusing part. He also skipped the kicker completely, which is honestly the most defensible thing here.

teams.teaser: Colin bought five tight ends, two of them older than the concept of the position mattering.
body: Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Saquon, Javonte Williams. Clean, strong, boring in the good way. Then round seven arrives and Colin takes Travis Kelce, entering his age-36 season, and immediately follows him with Mark Andrews, who's spent every recent January being asked what happened. Two picks, back to back, both tight ends, both guys whose best football is a memory.

He wasn't done. Isaiah Likely in the ninth — Andrews's own backup, so Colin now owns both halves of one job — and AJ Barner in the thirteenth. Five tight ends. One slot. The museum has a west wing and nobody's visiting either.

Quarterback is Jordan Love and Malik Willis, which is Love and Love's actual backup in Green Bay. Colin's superflex plan is to start a guy and then start the guy who plays when that guy can't, at the same time, which can't happen. Tony Pollard in the sixth and Jerry Jeudy in the twelfth are the kind of picks you make when the good part of the draft is over and you're still holding a card. He skipped the kicker, so at least one position on this roster was spared.

teams.teaser: James built a receiving corps deep enough to field two teams, then gave the ball to Derrick Henry.
body: Derrick Henry at 1.09 is a bet that a 31-year-old running back keeps defying the actuarial tables, and James made it first thing, before the coffee. Joe Burrow next, and then the receiver collection begins and never really stops: Garrett Wilson, Emeka Egbuka, Luther Burden, Michael Wilson, Matthew Golden, Jordan Addison. Six of them after the fifth round alone. Three slots.

Michael Wilson in the ninth is the one to sit with. James looked at a board full of startable players, found the third option in Arizona, and took him twenty-six spots early because something in the tape spoke to him. Then he did it again in the eleventh with MarShawn Lloyd, a guy whose NFL career so far is mostly a training room. The bench is a scouting hunch with a jersey on.

Burrow is the only quarterback. Superflex starts two. James spent nine picks on pass catchers and one on the guy throwing to them, so half his lineup every week will be a receiver standing in a quarterback-shaped hole. Omarion Hampton and TreVeyon Henderson at least give Henry somewhere to hand off when the tread runs out. Oronde Gadsden in the thirteenth is the only tight end, which after the last few teams counts as restraint.

teams.verdict: Four tight ends, no running backs
teams.teaser: Justin took Harold Fannin in the fifth and then bought three more tight ends in case that one didn't work.
body: Amon-Ra, Lamar, Bo Nix. Genuinely strong through three, and the quarterback room is the only fully solved one in the league. Then round five, and Justin takes Harold Fannin Jr., a rookie tight end, thirteen better players early, because somebody told him about a training camp rep and he never recovered from it.

Dallas Goedert follows in the eighth, Dalton Schultz in the twelfth. Three tight ends for one slot, and none of them are the kind you build around — they're the kind you stream, collected like a set. The bench is going to be two guys watching a third guy catch four passes for thirty yards.

Running back is Quinshon Judkins and David Montgomery. Two slots, two bodies, no margin. Meanwhile Justin kept adding receivers — Rome Odunze, Christian Watson, Parker Washington, Brian Thomas, Chris Godwin — until the room hit six. Watson and Godwin are both coming off serious injuries and Justin took them anyway, one after Odunze and one in the thirteenth, quietly assembling the most optimistic depth chart on the page. No kicker. Just tight ends, all the way down.

teams.teaser: Mike drafted six quarterbacks in a format that starts two and then remembered somebody has to run the ball.
body: Jalen Hurts, Drake Maye, Dak Prescott, Jaxson Dart, Daniel Jones. Five quarterbacks in six rounds, and Dart's a rookie who has to win a job first. Mike wasn't building a lineup, he was negotiating against himself in a market with one bidder, and the bidder kept raising. Daniel Jones in the sixth is the pick where the collection stops being funny and starts being a hobby.

D'Andre Swift is the running back. Singular. Round five, and then Mike never went back. Two RB slots, one guy, and a bench stacked with passers who can't fill either. Every Sunday he'll stare at that empty second slot, then start a fifth quarterback in the flex and tell everyone it's by design.

Tee Higgins, Terry McLaurin, Jakobi Meyers, Jayden Reed and KC Concepcion give him a real receiver room, which makes the whole thing worse — there was a good team in here somewhere. Hunter Henry and Kenyon Sadiq handle tight end, and Sadiq's a rookie taken four spots ahead of better options because at that point Mike had stopped consulting anything. Take away the quarterbacks and this roster is eight players.

teams.teaser: Evan assembled the veterans' wing — Rodgers, Adams, Deebo — like a man shopping a going-out-of-business sale.
body: James Cook and De'Von Achane back to back, then Mahomes, then Brock Bowers. Four picks, four legitimate answers, and for a moment Evan looked like the smartest guy in the room. Then the second quarterback slot came due and he handled it in round eleven with Aaron Rodgers, entering his age-42 season, on his third team in four years. Superflex means that man starts every week.

The pattern repeats everywhere. Davante Adams in the sixth. Deebo Samuel in the thirteenth. Alec Pierce, whose job is running deep and hoping. Evan built a roster where half the starters have a Pro Bowl from a previous decade and the other half are still good. It's a locker room where the young guys have to hear the same story twice.

Three tight ends — Bowers, Hockenson, Freiermuth — for one slot, and Freiermuth arrived in the twelfth to sit behind two guys who'll never move. Rhamondre Stevenson and Jaylen Waddle fill out the middle just fine. He skipped the kicker, which is the correct call and also the only pick Evan made all night that nobody can argue with.
